title: A serotonergic interaction
prompt: A 39-year-old woman taking sertraline begins tramadol for pain. Two days later she develops agitation, sweating, diarrhea, fever, hyperreflexia, and inducible ankle clonus. There is no dopamine-blocking medication exposure. Which drug action most directly contributes to this syndrome?
options: Blockade of dopamine D2 receptors
Blockade of muscarinic receptors
Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase
Irreversible inhibition of cyclooxygenase
Inhibition of serotonin reuptake
explanation: Tramadol has serotonergic activity; combining it with an SSRI can cause serotonin toxicity.

distractorExplanations.Inhibition of serotonin reuptake: Tramadol has serotonergic activity; combining it with an SSRI can cause serotonin toxicity.
distractorExplanations.Blockade of dopamine D2 receptors: This would suggest neuroleptic malignant syndrome, typically with rigidity rather than prominent clonus.
distractorExplanations.Blockade of muscarinic receptors: Antimuscarinic toxicity typically causes dry skin and reduced bowel activity.
distractorExplanations.Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase: This mechanism produces cholinergic excess and is not tramadol’s action.
distractorExplanations.Irreversible inhibition of cyclooxygenas: This explains aspirin effects, not serotonin toxicity.

title: Unexpected opioid toxicity
prompt: A 26-year-old adult becomes profoundly sleepy with a respiratory rate of 7/min after prescribed tramadol doses. Emergency ventilatory support is started. Testing later identifies multiple functional copies of CYP2D6. Which finding best explains the unexpectedly strong opioid effect?
answer: Rapid formation of the active M1 metabolite
options: Accelerated renal removal of M1
Blockade of mu receptors by tramadol
Reduced absorption of the administered dose
Rapid formation of the active M1 metabolite
Failure to form any active metabolite
explanation: CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolism can increase active-metabolite exposure and respiratory toxicity.

distractorExplanations.Rapid formation of the active M1 metabol: CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolism can increase active-metabolite exposure and respiratory toxicity.
distractorExplanations.Failure to form any active metabolite: This does not explain enhanced metabolite-mediated opioid effects.
distractorExplanations.Accelerated renal removal of M1: More rapid removal would reduce exposure.
distractorExplanations.Blockade of mu receptors by tramadol: Opioid antagonism would not explain this toxidrome.
distractorExplanations.Reduced absorption of the administered d: Reduced absorption would generally lower exposure.

title: Seizure risk during analgesic selection
prompt: A 47-year-old man with epilepsy and a recent breakthrough seizure needs treatment for persistent pain. His clinician considers tramadol but reviews its neurologic adverse effects before prescribing. Which concern is especially relevant to this patient’s history?
options: Tramadol selectively abolishes absence seizures
Tramadol causes seizures only after years of use
Tramadol can provoke seizures
Tramadol reliably protects against focal seizures
Tramadol prevents seizures through dopamine blockade
explanation: Seizure risk is increased in patients with epilepsy or other seizure predispositions.

distractorExplanations.Tramadol can provoke seizures: Seizure risk is increased in patients with epilepsy or other seizure predispositions.
distractorExplanations.Tramadol reliably protects against focal: It is not an antiseizure medication.
distractorExplanations.Tramadol prevents seizures through dopam: Dopamine blockade is not its therapeutic mechanism.
distractorExplanations.Tramadol selectively abolishes absence s: This describes neither its indication nor its action.
distractorExplanations.Tramadol causes seizures only after year: Seizures are not restricted to long-term exposure.

title: A pediatric prescribing restriction
prompt: An 11-year-old child has pain after a fracture. During medication reconciliation, the pharmacist sees a proposed tramadol prescription. The child has normal renal function and no medication allergies. Which feature independently makes tramadol contraindicated under US labeling?
options: No previous opioid exposure
Age younger than 12 years
Normal renal function
Absence of drug allergies
A fracture as the source of pain
explanation: US tramadol labeling contraindicates use below age 12.

distractorExplanations.Age younger than 12 years: US tramadol labeling contraindicates use below age 12.
distractorExplanations.Normal renal function: Normal renal function is not a contraindication.
distractorExplanations.Absence of drug allergies: A negative allergy history is not a contraindication.
distractorExplanations.A fracture as the source of pain: The injury itself is not the age-based contraindication being tested.
distractorExplanations.No previous opioid exposure: The specific absolute restriction here is age; opioid-naive adults are not universally excluded.

title: Contrasting analgesic mechanisms
prompt: A medical student compares tramadol with a conventional pure mu-opioid agonist. Both can produce opioid adverse effects, but tramadol has an additional monoaminergic action relevant to analgesia and drug interactions. Which paired action correctly describes that additional mechanism?
answer: Reduced reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine
options: Reduced reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine
Increased reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine
Blockade of serotonin synthesis and dopamine synthesis
Direct activation of GABA-A and GABA-B receptors
Inhibition of histamine degradation and acetylcholine release
explanation: Tramadol also inhibits serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake.

distractorExplanations.Reduced reuptake of serotonin and norepi: Tramadol also inhibits serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake.
distractorExplanations.Blockade of serotonin synthesis and dopa: This is not its analgesic mechanism.
distractorExplanations.Direct activation of GABA-A and GABA-B r: These are not its characteristic monoaminergic targets.
distractorExplanations.Inhibition of histamine degradation and: This does not describe tramadol’s additional analgesic action.

title: Withdrawal immediately after induction
prompt: A 32-year-old man dependent on a full opioid agonist takes buprenorphine before developing withdrawal from his previous opioid. Soon afterward he develops yawning, piloerection, abdominal cramping, and diarrhea. Which receptor property best explains this abrupt deterioration?
answer: High-affinity mu-receptor binding with partial agonist activity
options: Full mu-receptor agonism with greater intrinsic activity
Irreversible destruction of mu receptors
Selective activation of peripheral muscarinic receptors
Increased metabolism of the prior opioid through enzyme induction
High-affinity mu-receptor binding with partial agonist activity
explanation: Replacing a full agonist with buprenorphine can abruptly reduce receptor activation and precipitate withdrawal.

distractorExplanations.High-affinity mu-receptor binding with p: Replacing a full agonist with buprenorphine can abruptly reduce receptor activation and precipitate withdrawal.
distractorExplanations.Full mu-receptor agonism with greater in: Greater agonist activation would not explain this abrupt withdrawal.
distractorExplanations.Irreversible destruction of mu receptors: Buprenorphine does not destroy opioid receptors.
distractorExplanations.Selective activation of peripheral musca: This does not explain the opioid-dependent induction setting.
distractorExplanations.Increased metabolism of the prior opioid: The immediate onset is better explained by receptor displacement.

title: Risk from a sedative combination
prompt: A 45-year-old woman receiving buprenorphine for opioid use disorder takes nonprescribed alprazolam and becomes difficult to awaken with slow breathing. Her respiratory rate is 8/min, and assisted ventilation is initiated. Which interpretation of this event is most accurate?
answer: Buprenorphine can cause serious respiratory depression, especially with CNS depressants
options: Alprazolam acts as an opioid antagonist
The combination reliably protects against sedation
Buprenorphine’s only respiratory effect is hyperventilation
Buprenorphine can cause serious respiratory depression, especially with CNS depressants
Partial agonism makes opioid respiratory depression impossible
explanation: Partial agonism does not eliminate respiratory risk, and benzodiazepines increase that risk.

distractorExplanations.Buprenorphine can cause serious respirat: Partial agonism does not eliminate respiratory risk, and benzodiazepines increase that risk.
distractorExplanations.Partial agonism makes opioid respiratory: This is a dangerous misconception; serious respiratory depression can occur.
distractorExplanations.Alprazolam acts as an opioid antagonist: It is a benzodiazepine, not an opioid antagonist.
distractorExplanations.The combination reliably protects agains: The drugs can instead have additive depressant effects.
distractorExplanations.Buprenorphine’s only respiratory effect: This contradicts the recognized opioid respiratory toxicity.

title: The antagonist in a combination product
prompt: A patient asks why an opioid antagonist is included in buprenorphine/naloxone sublingual treatment. The clinician explains that route of administration matters. In a person dependent on a full opioid agonist, which effect is associated with parenteral misuse of this combination?
options: Naloxone prevents all possible misuse by every route
Naloxone irreversibly inhibits CYP3A4
Naloxone can precipitate opioid withdrawal
Naloxone increases mu-receptor intrinsic activity
Naloxone converts buprenorphine into a full agonist
explanation: Parenteral naloxone can antagonize opioid receptors and provoke withdrawal.

distractorExplanations.Naloxone can precipitate opioid withdraw: Parenteral naloxone can antagonize opioid receptors and provoke withdrawal.
distractorExplanations.Naloxone increases mu-receptor intrinsic: Naloxone is an antagonist rather than an agonist enhancer.
distractorExplanations.Naloxone converts buprenorphine into a f: It does not change buprenorphine’s intrinsic activity.
distractorExplanations.Naloxone prevents all possible misuse by: The combination does not eliminate every form of misuse.
distractorExplanations.Naloxone irreversibly inhibits CYP3A4: Its relevant action is receptor antagonism, not this metabolic effect.

title: Responding to respiratory toxicity
prompt: An adult with suspected buprenorphine overdose has marked hypoventilation. Emergency personnel provide assisted ventilation. A trainee states that an opioid reversal agent can never help because buprenorphine binds receptors strongly. Which response best corrects that statement?
answer: Naloxone may help, but repeated or higher doses can be necessary
options: Assume a single ineffective dose proves there is no opioid toxicity
Naloxone may help, but repeated or higher doses can be necessary
Stop ventilation while awaiting spontaneous drug clearance
Use flumazenil as the specific buprenorphine antagonist
Give a full opioid agonist to displace buprenorphine
explanation: Ventilatory support is essential; reversal may require repeated or higher doses.

distractorExplanations.Naloxone may help, but repeated or highe: Ventilatory support is essential; reversal may require repeated or higher doses.
distractorExplanations.Stop ventilation while awaiting spontane: Airway and ventilatory support must not be withheld.
distractorExplanations.Use flumazenil as the specific buprenorp: Flumazenil targets benzodiazepine effects, not opioid receptors.
distractorExplanations.Give a full opioid agonist to displace b: This is not appropriate reversal therapy and can worsen toxicity.
distractorExplanations.Assume a single ineffective dose proves: Limited response to one dose does not exclude buprenorphine toxicity.

title: Symptoms after an unplanned interruption
prompt: A 38-year-old woman stable on buprenorphine treatment abruptly stops taking it. She later develops sweating, abdominal cramps, and restlessness. There is no fever or recent infectious exposure. Which pharmacologic principle best explains this presentation?
answer: Chronic partial agonist exposure can produce physical dependence
options: Chronic partial agonist exposure can produce physical dependence
Partial agonists never produce physical dependence
Withdrawal proves that prescribed treatment was ineffective
Physical dependence is identical to compulsive drug use
Abrupt cessation increases continuing mu-receptor activation
explanation: Buprenorphine can produce dependence and withdrawal after abrupt cessation.

distractorExplanations.Chronic partial agonist exposure can pro: Buprenorphine can produce dependence and withdrawal after abrupt cessation.
distractorExplanations.Partial agonists never produce physical: Partial agonist activity does not rule out dependence.
distractorExplanations.Withdrawal proves that prescribed treatm: Withdrawal reflects adaptation, not necessarily failure of treatment.
distractorExplanations.Physical dependence is identical to comp: Dependence and the behavioral disorder of addiction are distinct concepts.
distractorExplanations.Abrupt cessation increases continuing mu: Stopping exposure reduces, rather than increases, ongoing agonist activation.
